Phonons and related properties of extended systems
from density-functional perturbation theory

Stefano Baroni    Stefano de Gironcoli    Andrea Dal Corso Address: SISSA – Scuola Internazionale Superiore di Studi Avanzati and
INFM – Istituto Nazionale di Fisica della Materia
via Beirut 2-4, 34014 Trieste, Italy    Paolo Giannozzi∗ Address: Chemistry Department, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey 08544
Abstract

This article reviews the current status of lattice-dynamical calculations in crystals, using density-functional perturbation theory, with emphasis on the plane-wave pseudo-potential method. Several specialized topics are treated, including the implementation for metals, the calculation of the response to macroscopic electric fields and their relevance to long wave-length vibrations in polar materials, the response to strain deformations, and higher-order responses. The success of this methodology is demonstrated with a number of applications existing in the literature.

I Introduction

The theory of lattice vibrations is one of the best established chapters of modern solid state physics and very few of the astonishing successes met by the latter could have been achieved without a strong foundation of the former. A wide variety of physical properties of solids depend on their lattice-dynamical behavior: infrared, Raman, and neutron-diffraction spectra; specific heats, thermal expansion, and heat conduction; phenomena related to the electron-phonon interaction such as the resistivity of metals, super-conductivity, and the temperature dependence of optical spectra, are just a few of them. As a matter of fact, their understanding in terms of phonons is considered to be one of the most convincing evidences that our current quantum picture of solids is correct.

The basic theory of lattice vibrations dates back to the thirties and the treatise of ? is still considered today to be the reference textbook in this field. These early formulations were mainly concerned with establishing the general properties of the dynamical matrices—such as e.g. their symmetry and/or analytical properties—without even considering their connections with the electronic properties which actually determine them. A systematic study of these connections was not performed until the seventies [DeCicco, PCM]. The relationship between the electronic and the lattice-dynamical properties of a system is important not only as a matter of principle, but also because (and perhaps mainly because) it is only exploiting these relations that it is possible to calculate the lattice-dynamical properties of specific systems.

The state of the art of theoretical condensed-matter physics and of computational materials science is such that it is nowadays possible to calculate specific properties of specific (simple) materials using ab initio quantum mechanical techniques whose only input information is the chemical composition of the materials. In the specific case of lattice-dynamical properties, a large number of ab initio calculations based on the linear-response theory of lattice vibrations [DeCicco, PCM] have been made possible over the past 10 years by the achievements of density-functional theory [HK, KS], and by the development of density-functional perturbation theory [Zein1, BGT] which is a method to apply the former within the general theoretical framework provided by the latter. Thanks to these theoretical and algorithmic advances, it is now possible to obtain accurate phonon dispersions on a fine grid of wave-vectors covering the entire Brillouin zone, which compare directly with neutron diffraction data, and from which several physical properties of the system (such as heat capacities, thermal expansion coefficients, temperature dependence of the band gap, and so on) can be calculated.

The purpose of the present paper is to illustrate in some detail the theoretical framework of density-functional perturbation theory, including several technical details which are useful for its implementation within the plane-wave pseudo-potential scheme. We will also provide a representative, though necessarily incomplete, choice of significant applications to the physics of insulators and metals, including their surfaces, alloys, and micro-structures.

II Density-Functional Perturbation Theory

II.1 Lattice dynamics from electronic-structure theory

The basic approximation which allows one to decouple the vibrational from the electronic degrees of freedom in a solid is the adiabatic approximation by Born and Oppenheimer (BO) [Born-Oppenheimer]. Within this approximation, the lattice-dynamical properties of a system are determined by the eigenvalues ℰ{\cal E} and eigenfunctions Φ\Phi of the Schrödinger equation:

(−∑Iℏ22​MI∂2∂𝐑I2+E(𝐑))Φ(𝐑)=ℰΦ(𝐑),\left(-\sum_{I}{\hbar^{2}\over 2M_{I}}{\partial^{2}\over\partial{\bf R}_{I}^{2}}+E({\bf R})\right)\Phi({\bf R})={\cal E}\Phi({\bf R}), (1)

where 𝐑I{\bf R}_{I} is the coordinate of the II-th nucleus, MIM_{I} its mass, 𝐑≡{𝐑I}{\bf R}\equiv\{{\bf R}_{I}\} indicates the set of all the nuclear coordinates, and E⁡(𝐑)E({\bf R}) is the clamped-ion energy of the system, which is often referred to as the Born-Oppenheimer energy surface. In practice, E⁡(𝐑)E({\bf R}) is the ground-state energy of a system of interacting electrons moving in the field of fixed nuclei, whose Hamiltonian—which acts onto the electronic variables and depends parametrically upon 𝐑{\bf R}—reads:

HB​O(𝐑)=−ℏ22​m∑i∂2∂𝐫i2+e22∑i≠j1|𝐫i−𝐫j|\hfil\displaystyle\quad H_{BO}({\bf R})=-{\hbar^{2}\over 2m}\sum_{i}{\partial^{2}\over\partial{\bf r}_{i}^{2}}+{e^{2}\over 2}\sum_{i\neq j}{1\over|{\bf r}_{i}-{\bf r}_{j}|}\hfill
−∑i​IZI​e2|𝐫i−𝐑I|+EN(𝐑),(2)\hfil\displaystyle\hfill-\sum_{iI}{Z_{I}e^{2}\over|{\bf r}_{i}-{\bf R}_{I}|}+E_{N}({\bf R}),\quad(2)

where ZIZ_{I} is the charge of the II-th nucleus, −e-e is the electron charge, and EN​(𝐑)E_{N}({\bf R}) is the electrostatic interaction between different nuclei:

EN​(𝐑)=e22​∑I≠JZI​ZJ|𝐑I−𝐑J|.E_{N}({\bf R})={e^{2}\over 2}\sum_{I\neq J}{Z_{I}Z_{J}\over|{\bf R}_{I}-{\bf R}_{J}|}. (3)

The equilibrium geometry of the system is given by the condition that the forces acting on individual nuclei vanish:

𝐅I≡−∂E⁡(𝐑)∂𝐑I=0,{\bf F}_{I}\equiv-{\partial E({\bf R})\over\partial{\bf R}_{I}}=0, (4)

whereas the vibrational frequencies, ω\omega, are determined by the eigenvalues of the Hessian of the BO energy, scaled by the nuclear masses:

det​|1MI​MJ​∂2E⁡(𝐑)∂𝐑I​∂𝐑J−ω2|=0.{\rm det}\left|{1\over\sqrt{M_{I}M_{J}}}{\partial^{2}E({\bf R})\over\partial{\bf R}_{I}\partial{\bf R}_{J}}-\omega^{2}\right|=0. (5)

The calculation of the equilibrium geometry and of the vibrational properties of a system thus amounts to computing the first and second derivatives of its BO energy surface. The basic tool to accomplish this goal is the Hellmann-Feynman (HF) theorem [Hellmann, Feynman] which states that the first derivative of the eigenvalues of a Hamiltonian that depends on a parameter λ\lambda, HλH_{\lambda}, is given by the expectation value of the derivative of the Hamiltonian:

∂Eλ∂λ=⟨Ψλ​|∂Hλ∂λ|​Ψλ⟩,{\partial E_{\lambda}\over\partial\lambda}=\left\langle\Psi_{\lambda}\left|{\partial H_{\lambda}\over\partial\lambda}\right|\Psi_{\lambda}\right\rangle, (6)

where Ψλ\Psi_{\lambda} is the eigenfunction of HλH_{\lambda} corresponding to the EλE_{\lambda} eigenvalue: Hλ​Ψλ=Eλ​ΨλH_{\lambda}\Psi_{\lambda}=E_{\lambda}\Psi_{\lambda}. In the BO approximation, nuclear coordinates act as parameters in the electronic Hamiltonian, Eq. (II.1). The force acting on the II-th nucleus in the electronic ground state is thus:

𝐅I=−∂E⁡(𝐑)∂𝐑I=−⟨Ψ⁡(𝐑)​|∂HB​O​(𝐑)∂𝐑I|​Ψ​(𝐑)⟩,{\bf F}_{I}=-{\partial E({\bf R})\over\partial{\bf R}_{I}}=-\left\langle\Psi({\bf R})\left|{\partial H_{BO}({\bf R})\over\partial{\bf R}_{I}}\right|\Psi({\bf R})\right\rangle, (7)

where Ψ⁡(𝐫,𝐑)\Psi({\bf r},{\bf R}) is the electronic ground-state wave-function of the BO Hamiltonian. The BO Hamiltonian depends on 𝐑{\bf R} via the electron-ion interaction that couples to the electronic degrees of freedom only through the electron charge density. The HF theorem states in this case that:

𝐅I=−∫n𝐑(𝐫)∂V𝐑​(𝐫)∂𝐑Id𝐫−∂EN​(𝐑)∂𝐑I,{\bf F}_{I}=-\int n_{\bf R}({\bf r}){\partial V_{\bf R}({\bf r})\over\partial{\bf R}_{I}}d{\bf r}-{\partial E_{N}({\bf R})\over\partial{\bf R}_{I}}, (8)

where V𝐑​(𝐫)V_{\bf R}({\bf r}) is the electron-nucleus interaction,

V𝐑(𝐫)=−∑i​IZI​e2|𝐫i−𝐑I|,V_{\bf R}({\bf r})=-\sum_{iI}{Z_{I}e^{2}\over|{\bf r}_{i}-{\bf R}_{I}|}, (9)

and n𝐑​(𝐫)n_{\bf R}({\bf r}) is the ground-state electron charge density corresponding to the nuclear configuration 𝐑{\bf R}. The Hessian of the BO energy surface appearing in Eq. (5) is obtained by differentiating the HF forces with respect to nuclear coordinates:

∂2E⁡(𝐑)∂𝐑I​∂𝐑J≡−∂𝐅I∂𝐑J=∫∂n𝐑​(𝐫)∂𝐑J​∂V𝐑​(𝐫)∂𝐑I​𝑑𝐫\hfil\displaystyle\quad{\partial^{2}E({\bf R})\over\partial{\bf R}_{I}\partial{\bf R}_{J}}\equiv-{\partial{\bf F}_{I}\over\partial{\bf R}_{J}}=\int{\partial n_{\bf R}({\bf r})\over\partial{\bf R}_{J}}{\partial V_{\bf R}({\bf r})\over\partial{\bf R}_{I}}d{\bf r}\hfill
+∫n𝐑(𝐫)∂2V𝐑​(𝐫)∂𝐑I​∂𝐑Jd𝐫+∂2EN​(𝐑)∂𝐑I​∂𝐑J.(10)\hfil\displaystyle\hfill+\int n_{\bf R}({\bf r}){\partial^{2}V_{\bf R}({\bf r})\over\partial{\bf R}_{I}\partial{\bf R}_{J}}d{\bf r}+{\partial^{2}E_{N}({\bf R})\over\partial{\bf R}_{I}\partial{\bf R}_{J}}.\quad(10)

Eq. (II.1) states that the calculation of the Hessian of the BO energy surfaces requires the calculation of the ground-state electron charge density, n𝐑​(𝐫)n_{\bf R}({\bf r}), as well as of its linear response to a distortion of the nuclear geometry, ∂n𝐑​(𝐫)/∂𝐑I{\partial n_{\bf R}({\bf r})/\partial{\bf R}_{I}}. This fundamental result was first stated in the late sixties by ? and ?. The Hessian matrix is usually called the matrix of the inter-atomic force constants (IFC).

II.2 Density Functional Theory

According to the preceding discussion, the calculation of the derivatives of the BO energy surface with respect to the nuclear coordinates only requires the knowledge of the electronic charge-density distribution. This fact is a special case of a much more general property of the systems of interacting electrons, known as the ? theorem. According to this theorem, no two different potentials acting on the electrons of a given system can give rise to a same ground-state electronic charge density. This property can be used in conjunction with the standard Rayleigh-Ritz variational principle of quantum mechanics to show that a universal functional,11 1 By universal it is meant here that the functional is independent of the external potential acting on the electrons, though it obviously depends on the form of the electron-electron interaction. F⁡[n⁡(𝐫)]F[n({\bf r})], of the electron charge density exists such that the functional:

E⁡[n⁡(𝐫)]=F⁡[n⁡(𝐫)]+∫n⁡(𝐫)​V​(𝐫)​𝑑𝐫E[n({\bf r})]=F[n({\bf r})]+\int n({\bf r})V({\bf r})d{\bf r} (11)

is minimized by the electron charge density of the ground state corresponding to the external potential V⁡(𝐫)V({\bf r}), under the constraint that the integral of n⁡(𝐫)n({\bf r}) equals the total number of electrons. Furthermore, the value of the minimum coincides with the ground-state energy. This theorem provides the foundation of what is currently known as density-functional theory (DFT) [DFT1, DFT2]. It allows an enormous conceptual simplification of the quantum-mechanical problem of the search of the ground-state properties of a system of interacting electrons, for it replaces the traditional description based on wave-functions (which depend on 3​N3N independent variables, NN being the number of electrons) with a much more tractable description in terms of the charge density, which only depends on 3 variables. Two major problems hamper a straightforward application of this remarkably simple result: the fact that the form of the FF functional is unknown, and that the conditions to be fulfilled for a function n⁡(𝐫)n({\bf r}) to be considered an acceptable ground-state charge distribution (and hence the domain of the functional FF) are poorly characterized. The second problem is hardly addressed at all, and one usually contents oneself to impose the proper normalization of the charge density by the use of a Lagrange multiplier. The first problem can be handled by mapping the system onto an auxiliary system of non interacting electrons [KS] and by making appropriate approximations along the lines described in the next subsection.

II.2.1 The Kohn-Sham equations

The Hohenberg and Kohn theorem states that all the physical properties of a system of interacting electrons are uniquely determined by its ground-state charge-density distribution. This property holds independently of the precise form of the electron-electron interaction. In particular, when the strength of the electron-electron interaction vanishes, F⁡[n⁡(𝐫)]F[n({\bf r})] defines the ground-state kinetic energy of a system of non-interacting electrons as a functional of its ground-state charge-density distribution, T0​[n​(𝐫)]T_{0}[n({\bf r})]. This fact has been used by ? to map the problem of a system of interacting electrons onto an equivalent non-interacting problem. To this end, the unknown functional F⁡[n⁡(𝐫)]F[n({\bf r})] is cast into the form:

F⁡[n⁡(𝐫)]=T0​[n⁡(𝐫)]+e22​∫n⁡(𝐫)​n​(𝐫′)|𝐫−𝐫′|​𝑑𝐫​d​𝐫′\hfil\displaystyle\quad F[n({\bf r})]=T_{0}[n({\bf r})]+{e^{2}\over 2}\int{n({\bf r})n({\bf r}^{\prime})\over|{\bf r}-{\bf r}^{\prime}|}d{\bf r}d{\bf r}^{\prime}\hfill
+Ex​c​[n⁡(𝐫)],(12)\hfil\displaystyle\hfill+E_{xc}[n({\bf r})],\quad(12)

where the second term is the classical electrostatic self-interaction of the electron charge-density distribution, and the so-called exchange-correlation energy, Ex​cE_{xc}, is defined by Eq. (II.2.1).22 2 The exchange-correlation energy is the name we give to the part of the energy functional that we do not know how to calculate otherwise. For this reason, it has been named stupidity energy by ?. Whether or not this is an useful concept depends on its magnitude with respect to the total functional and on the quality of the approximations one can find for it. Variation of the energy functional with respect to n⁡(𝐫)n({\bf r}) with the constraint that the number of electrons is kept fixed leads formally to the same equation that would hold for a system of non-interacting electrons subject to an effective potential (also called self-consistent, SCF, potential) whose form is:

VS​C​F​(𝐫)=V⁡(𝐫)+e2​∫n⁡(𝐫′)|𝐫−𝐫′|​d​𝐫′+vx​c​(𝐫),V_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}({\bf r})=V({\bf r})+e^{2}\int{n({\bf r}^{\prime})\over|{\bf r}-{\bf r}^{\prime}|}d{\bf r}^{\prime}+v_{xc}({\bf r}), (13)

where

vx​c​(𝐫)≡δ​Ex​cδ​n​(𝐫)v_{xc}({\bf r})\equiv{\delta E_{xc}\over\delta n({\bf r})} (14)

is the functional derivative of the exchange-correlation energy, also called the exchange-correlation potential.

The power of this trick is that, if one knew the effective potential VS​C​F​(𝐫)V_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}({\bf r}), the problem for non-interacting electrons could be trivially solved without knowing the form of the non-interacting kinetic-energy functional, T0T_{0}. To this end, one should simply solve the one-electron Schrödinger equation:

(−ℏ22​m​∂2∂𝐫2+VS​C​F​(𝐫))​ψn​(𝐫)=ϵn​ψn​(𝐫).\left(-{\hbar^{2}\over 2m}{\partial^{2}\over\partial{\bf r}^{2}}+V_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}({\bf r})\right)\psi_{n}({\bf r})=\epsilon_{n}\psi_{n}({\bf r}). (15)

The ground-state charge-density distribution and non-interacting kinetic energy functional would then be given in terms of the auxiliary Kohn-Sham (KS) orbitals, ψn​(𝐫)\psi_{n}({\bf r}):

n⁡(𝐫)\displaystyle n({\bf r}) =\displaystyle= 2​∑n=1N/2|ψn​(𝐫)|2\displaystyle 2\sum_{n=1}^{N/2}|\psi_{n}({\bf r})|^{2} (16)
T0​[n​(𝐫)]\displaystyle T_{0}[n({\bf r})] =\displaystyle= −2ℏ22​m∑n=1N/2∫ψn∗(𝐫)∂2ψn​(𝐫)∂𝐫2d𝐫,\displaystyle-2{\hbar^{2}\over 2m}\sum_{n=1}^{N/2}\int\psi^{*}_{n}({\bf r}){\partial^{2}\psi_{n}({\bf r})\over\partial{\bf r}^{2}}d{\bf r}, (17)

where NN is the number of electrons, and the system is supposed to be non-magnetic, so that each one of the N/2N/2 lowest-lying orbital states accommodates 2 electrons of opposite spin. In periodic systems the index nn running over occupied states can be thought as a double label, n≡{v,𝐤}n\equiv\{v,{\bf k}\}, where vv indicates the set of valence bands, and 𝐤{\bf k} is a wave-vector belonging to the first Brillouin zone (BZ).

The ground-state energy given by Eqs. (11,II.2.1) can be equivalently expressed in terms of the KS eigenvalues:

E⁡[n⁡(𝐫)]=2​∑n=1N/2ϵn−e22​∫n⁡(𝐫)​n​(𝐫′)|𝐫−𝐫′|​𝑑𝐫​d​𝐫′\hfil\displaystyle\quad E[n({\bf r})]=2\sum_{n=1}^{N/2}\epsilon_{n}-{e^{2}\over 2}\int{n({\bf r})n({\bf r}^{\prime})\over|{\bf r}-{\bf r}^{\prime}|}d{\bf r}d{\bf r}^{\prime}\hfill
+Ex​c​[n⁡(𝐫)]−∫n⁡(𝐫)​vx​c​(𝐫)​𝑑𝐫.(18)\hfil\displaystyle\hfill+E_{xc}[n({\bf r})]-\int n({\bf r})v_{xc}({\bf r})d{\bf r}.\quad(18)

Eq. (15) has the form of a non-linear Schrödinger equation whose potential depends on its own eigenfunctions through the electron charge-density distribution. Once an explicit form for the exchange-correlation energy is available, this equation can be solved in a self-consistent way using a variety of methods.

II.2.2 Local-Density Approximation and beyond

The Kohn-Sham scheme constitutes a practical way to implement DFT, provided an accurate and reasonably easy-to-use approximation is available for the exchange-correlation energy, Ex​c​[n​(𝐫)]E_{xc}[n({\bf r})]. In their original paper, ? proposed to assume that each small volume of the system (so small that the charge density can be thought to be constant therein) contributes the same exchange-correlation energy as an equal volume of a homogeneous electron gas at the same density. With this assumption, the exchange-correlation energy functional and potential read:

Ex​c​[n​(𝐫)]\displaystyle E_{xc}[n({\bf r})] =\displaystyle= ∫ϵx​c​(n⁡(𝐫))​n​(𝐫)​𝑑𝐫,\displaystyle\int\epsilon_{xc}(n({\bf r}))n({\bf r})d{\bf r}, (19)
vx​c​(n​(𝐫))\displaystyle v_{xc}(n({\bf r})) =\displaystyle= (ϵx​c​(n)+n​d​ϵx​c​(n)d​n)n=n⁡(𝐫),\displaystyle\left(\epsilon_{xc}(n)+n{d\epsilon_{xc}(n)\over dn}\right)_{n=n({\bf r})}, (20)

where ϵx​c​(n)\epsilon_{xc}(n) is the exchange-correlation energy per particle in an homogeneous electron gas at density nn. This approximation is known as the local density approximation (LDA). Approximate forms for ϵx​c​(n)\epsilon_{xc}(n) have been known for a long time. Numerical results from nearly exact Monte-Carlo calculations for the homogeneous electron gas by ? have been parameterized by ? with a simple analytical form. More accurate parameterizations have been recently proposed by ?. All these different forms are very similar in the range of electron densities relevant to condensed-matter applications and yield very similar results.

The LDA is exact in the limit of high density or of a slowly varying charge-density distribution [KS]. LDA has turned out to be much more successful than originally expected (see for instance ?), in spite of its extreme simplicity. For weakly correlated materials, such as semiconductors and simple metals, LDA accurately describes structural and vibrational properties: the correct structure is usually found to have the lowest energy, while bond lengths, bulk moduli, and phonon frequencies are accurate within a few percent.

LDA also has some well-known drawbacks. A large overestimate (∼20\sim 20%) of the crystal cohesive and molecular binding energies is possibly the worst failure of this approximation, together with its inability to properly describe strongly correlated systems, such as e.g. transition-metal oxides. Much effort has been put in the search for better functionals than LDA (see for instance ?). The use of gradient corrections [Becke, PBE] to LDA has become widespread in recent years. Gradient corrections are generally found to improve the account of electron correlations in finite or semi-infinite systems, such as molecules or surfaces; less so in infinite solids.

In general, DFT is a ground-state theory and KS eigenvalues and eigenvector do not have a well defined physical meaning. Nevertheless, in the lack of better and equally general methods, KS eigenvalues are often used to estimate excitation energies. The general features of the low-lying energy bands in solids obtained in this way are generally considered to be at least qualitatively correct, in spite of the fact that the LDA is known to substantially underestimate the optical gaps in insulators.

II.3 Linear response

In Sec. II.1 we have seen that the electron-density linear response of a system determines the matrix of its IFC’s, Eq. (II.1). Let us see now how this response can be obtained within DFT. The procedure described in the following is usually referred to as density-functional perturbation theory (DFPT) [Zein1, BGT, Gonze2].

In order to simplify the notation and make the argument more general, we assume that the external potential acting on the electrons is a differentiable function of a set of parameters, λ≡{λi}{\boldmath{\lambda}}\equiv\{\lambda_{i}\} (λi≡𝐑I\lambda_{i}\equiv{\bf R}_{I} in the case of lattice dynamics). According to the HF theorem, the first and second derivatives of the ground-state energy read:

∂E∂λi\displaystyle{\partial E\over\partial\lambda_{i}} =\displaystyle= ∫∂Vλ​(𝐫)∂λi​nλ​(𝐫)​𝑑𝐫,\displaystyle\int{\partial V_{\boldmath\lambda}({\bf r})\over\partial\lambda_{i}}n_{\boldmath\lambda}({\bf r})d{\bf r}, (21)
∂2E∂λi​∂λj\displaystyle{\partial^{2}E\over\partial\lambda_{i}\partial\lambda_{j}} =\displaystyle= ∫∂2Vλ​(𝐫)∂λi​∂λj​nλ​(𝐫)​𝑑𝐫\displaystyle\int{\partial^{2}V_{\boldmath\lambda}({\bf r})\over\partial\lambda_{i}\partial\lambda_{j}}n_{\boldmath\lambda}({\bf r})d{\bf r} (22)
+∫∂nλ​(𝐫)∂λi​∂Vλ​(𝐫)∂λj​𝑑𝐫.\displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\mbox{}+\int{\partial n_{\boldmath\lambda}({\bf r})\over\partial\lambda_{i}}{\partial V_{\boldmath\lambda}({\bf r})\over\partial\lambda_{j}}d{\bf r}.

The electron-density response, ∂nλ​(𝐫)/∂λi{\partial n_{\boldmath\lambda}({\bf r})/\partial\lambda_{i}}, appearing in Eq. (22) can be evaluated by linearizing Eqs. (16), (15), and (13) with respect to wave-function, density, and potential variations. Linearization of Eq. (16) leads to:

Δ​n​(𝐫)=4​Re​∑n=1N/2ψn∗​(𝐫)​Δ​ψn​(𝐫),\Delta n({\bf r})=4~{\rm Re}\sum_{n=1}^{N/2}\psi_{n}^{*}({\bf r})\Delta\psi_{n}({\bf r}), (23)

where the finite-difference operator Δλ\Delta^{\lambda} is defined as:

Δλ​F=∑i∂Fλ∂λi​Δ​λi.\Delta^{\lambda}F=\sum_{i}{\partial F_{\lambda}\over\partial\lambda_{i}}\Delta\lambda_{i}. (24)

The super-script λ\lambda has been omitted in Eq. (23), as well as in any subsequent formulas where such an omission does not give rise to ambiguities. Since the external potential (both unperturbed and perturbed) is real, each KS eigenfunction and its complex conjugate are degenerate. As a consequence, the imaginary part of the sum appearing in Eq. (23) vanishes, so that the prescription to keep only the real part can be dropped.

The variation of the KS orbitals, Δ​ψn​(𝐫)\Delta\psi_{n}({\bf r}), is obtained by standard first-order perturbation theory [messiah]:

(HS​C​F−ϵn)​|Δ​ψn⟩=−(Δ​VS​C​F−Δ​ϵn)​|ψn⟩,(H_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}-\epsilon_{n})|\Delta\psi_{n}\rangle=-(\Delta V_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}-\Delta\epsilon_{n})|\psi_{n}\rangle, (25)

where

HS​C​F=−ℏ22​m​∂2∂𝐫2+VS​C​F​(𝐫)H_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}=-{\hbar^{2}\over 2m}{\partial^{2}\over\partial{\bf r}^{2}}+V_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}({\bf r}) (26)

is the unperturbed KS Hamiltonian,

Δ​VS​C​F​(𝐫)=Δ​V​(𝐫)+e2​∫Δ​n​(𝐫′)|𝐫−𝐫′|​d​𝐫′\hfil\displaystyle\quad\Delta V_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}({\bf r})=\Delta V({\bf r})+e^{2}\int{\Delta n({\bf r}^{\prime})\over|{\bf r}-{\bf r}^{\prime}|}d{\bf r}^{\prime}\hfill
+d​vx​c​(n)d​n|n=n⁡(𝐫)​Δ​n​(𝐫),(27)\hfil\displaystyle\hfill+\left.{dv_{xc}(n)\over dn}\right|_{n=n({\bf r})}\Delta n({\bf r}),\quad(27)

is the first-order correction to the self-consistent potential, and Δ​ϵn=⟨ψn|Δ​VS​C​F|ψn⟩\Delta\epsilon_{n}=\langle\psi_{n}|\Delta V_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}|\psi_{n}\rangle is the first order variation of the KS eigenvalue, ϵn\epsilon_{n}.

In the atomic physics literature, an equation analogous to Eq. (25) is known as the Sternheimer equation, after the work in which it was first used to calculate atomic polarizabilities [Sternheimer]. A self-consistent version of the Sternheimer equation was introduced by ? to calculate atomic polarizabilities within DFT in the LDA. Similar methods are known in the quantum chemistry literature under the generic name of analytic evaluation of second-order energy derivatives [CHF, Amos]. In the specific context of the Hartree-Fock approximation, the resulting algorithm is called the coupled Hartree-Fock method [CHF].

Equations (23–II.3) form a set of self-consistent equations for the perturbed system completely analogous to the KS equations in the unperturbed case—Eqs. (13), (15), and (16)—with the KS eigenvalue equation, Eq. (15), being replaced by the solution of a linear system, Eq. (25). In the present case, the self-consistency requirement manifests itself in the dependence of the right-hand side upon the solution of the linear system. As Δ​VS​C​F​(𝐫)\Delta V_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}({\bf r}) is a linear functional of Δ​n​(𝐫)\Delta n({\bf r}) which in turn depends linearly on the Δ​ψ\Delta\psi’s, the whole self-consistent calculation can be cast in terms of a generalized linear problem. Note however that the right-hand side of Eq. (25) for Δ​ψn\Delta\psi_{n} depends through Δ​n\Delta n on the solution of all the similar equations holding for the Δ​ψm\Delta\psi_{m} (m≠nm\neq n). Hence, all the NN equations, Eq. (25), are linearly coupled to each other, and the set of all the Δ​ψ\Delta\psi’s is the solution of a linear problem whose dimension is (N​M/2×N​M/2NM/2\times NM/2), MM being the size of the basis set used to describe the ψ\psi’s. The explicit form of this big linear equation can be worked out directly from Eqs. (23–II.3), or it can be equivalently derived from a variational principle, as explained in Sec. II.3.3. Whether this big linear system is better solved directly by iterative methods or by the self-consistent solution of the smaller linear systems given by Eq. (25) is a matter of computational strategy.

The first-order correction to a given eigen-function of the Schrödinger equation, given by Eq. (25), is often expressed in terms of a sum over the spectrum of the unperturbed Hamiltonian,

Δ​ψn​(𝐫)=∑m≠nψm​(𝐫)​⟨ψm|Δ​VS​C​F|ψn⟩ϵn−ϵm,\Delta\psi_{n}({\bf r})=\sum_{m\neq n}\psi_{m}({\bf r}){\langle\psi_{m}|\Delta V_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}|\psi_{n}\rangle\over\epsilon_{n}-\epsilon_{m}}, (28)

running over all the states of the system, occupied and empty, with the exception of the state being considered, for which the energy denominator would vanish. Using Eq. (28), the electron charge-density response, Eq. (23), can be cast into the form:

Δ​n​(𝐫)=4​∑n=1N/2∑m≠nψn∗​(𝐫)​ψm​(𝐫)​⟨ψm|Δ​VS​C​F|ψn⟩ϵn−ϵm.\Delta n({\bf r})=4\sum_{n=1}^{N/2}\sum_{m\neq n}\psi_{n}^{*}({\bf r})\psi_{m}({\bf r}){\langle\psi_{m}|\Delta V_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}|\psi_{n}\rangle\over\epsilon_{n}-\epsilon_{m}}. (29)

Eq. (29) shows that the contributions to the electron-density response coming from products of occupied states cancel each other, so that the mm index can be thought as running onto conduction states only. This is equivalent to say that the electron-density distribution does not respond to a perturbation which only acts onto the occupied-state manifold (or, more generally, to the component of any perturbation which couples occupied states among each other).

The explicit evaluation of Δ​ψn​(𝐫)\Delta\psi_{n}({\bf r}) from Eq. (28) would require the knowledge of the full spectrum of the KS Hamiltonian and extensive summations over conduction bands. In Eq. (25), instead, only the knowledge of the occupied states of the system is needed to construct the right-hand side of the equation, and efficient iterative algorithms—such as conjugate gradient [NumRec, CG, Payne] or minimal residual [NumRec, GMRES] methods—can be used for the solution of the linear system. In this way the computational cost of the determination of the density response to a single perturbation is of the same order as that needed for the calculation of the unperturbed ground-state density.

The left-hand side of Eq. (25) is singular because the linear operator appearing therein has a null eigenvalue. However, we saw above that the response of the system to an external perturbation only depends on the component of the perturbation which couples the occupied-state manifold with the empty-state one. The projection onto the empty-state manifold of the first-order correction to occupied orbitals can be obtained from Eq. (25) by replacing its right-hand side with −Pc​Δ​VS​C​F​|ψn⟩-P_{c}\Delta V_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}|\psi_{n}\rangle, where PcP_{c} is the projector onto the empty-state manifold, and by adding to the linear operator on its left-hand side, HS​C​F−ϵnH_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}-\epsilon_{n}, a multiple of the projector onto the occupied-state manifold, PvP_{v}, so as to make it non-singular:

(HS​C​F+α​Pv−ϵn)​|Δ​ψn⟩=−Pc​Δ​VS​C​F​|ψn⟩.(H_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}+\alpha P_{v}-\epsilon_{n})|\Delta\psi_{n}\rangle=-P_{c}\Delta V_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}|\psi_{n}\rangle. (30)

In practice, if the linear system is solved by the conjugate-gradient or any other iterative method and the trial solution is chosen orthogonal to the occupied-state manifold, orthogonality is maintained during iteration without having to care about the extra PvP_{v} term on the left-hand side of Eq. (30).

The above discussion applies to insulators where the gap is finite. In metals a finite density of states (DOS) occurs at the Fermi energy, and a change in the orbital occupation number may occur upon the application of an infinitesimal perturbation. The modifications of DFPT needed to treat the linear response of metals have been discussed by ? and will be presented in some detail in Sec. II.3.4.

II.3.1 Monochromatic perturbations

One of the greatest advantages of DFPT—as compared to other non-perturbative methods to calculate the vibrational properties of crystalline solids (such as, e.g. the frozen phonon or the molecular-dynamics spectral analysis methods)—is that within DFPT the responses to perturbations of different wave-lengths are decoupled. This feature allows one to calculate phonon frequencies at arbitrary wave-vectors 𝐪{\bf q} avoiding the use of super-cells and with a workload which is essentially independent of the phonon wave-length. To see this in some detail, we first rewrite Eq. (30) by explicitly indicating the wave-vector 𝐤{\bf k} and band index vv of the unperturbed wave-function, ψv𝐤\psi_{v}^{\bf k}, and by projecting both sides of the equation over the manifold of states of wave-vector 𝐤+𝐪{\bf k}+{\bf q}. Translational invariance requires that the projector onto the 𝐤+𝐪{\bf k}+{\bf q} manifold, P𝐤+𝐪P^{{\bf k}+{\bf q}}, commutes with HS​C​FH_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}} and with the projectors onto the occupied- and empty-state manifolds, PvP_{v} and PcP_{c}. By indicating with P𝐤+𝐪​Pv=Pv𝐤+𝐪P^{{\bf k}+{\bf q}}P_{v}=P^{{\bf k}+{\bf q}}_{v} and P𝐤+𝐪​Pc=Pc𝐤+𝐪P^{{\bf k}+{\bf q}}P_{c}=P^{{\bf k}+{\bf q}}_{c} the projectors onto the occupied and empty states of wave-vector 𝐤+𝐪{\bf k}+{\bf q}, Eq. (30) can be rewritten as:

(HS​C​F+α​Pv𝐤+𝐪−ϵv𝐤)​|Δ​ψv𝐤+𝐪⟩=\hfil\displaystyle\quad\left(H_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}+\alpha P^{{\bf k}+{\bf q}}_{v}-\epsilon_{v}^{\bf k}\right)|\Delta\psi_{v}^{{\bf k}+{\bf q}}\rangle=\hfill
−Pc𝐤+𝐪​Δ​VS​C​F​|ψv𝐤⟩,(31)\hfil\displaystyle\hfill-P^{{\bf k}+{\bf q}}_{c}\Delta V_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}|\psi_{v}^{\bf k}\rangle,\quad(31)

where |Δ​ψv𝐤+𝐪⟩=P𝐤+𝐪​|Δ​ψv𝐤⟩|\Delta\psi_{v}^{{\bf k}+{\bf q}}\rangle=P^{{\bf k}+{\bf q}}|\Delta\psi_{v}^{\bf k}\rangle. By decomposing the perturbing potential, Δ​VS​C​F\Delta V_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}, into Fourier components,

Δ​VS​C​F​(𝐫)=∑𝐪Δ​vS​C​F𝐪​(𝐫)​ei​𝐪⋅𝐫,\Delta V_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}({\bf r})=\sum_{\bf q}\Delta v_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}^{\bf q}({\bf r}){\rm e}^{i{\bf q}\cdot{\bf r}}, (32)

where Δ​vS​C​F𝐪​(𝐫)\Delta v_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}^{\bf q}({\bf r}) is a lattice-periodic function, Eq. (II.3.1) can be cast into the form:

(HS​C​F𝐤+𝐪+α​∑v′|uv′𝐤+𝐪⟩​⟨uv′𝐤+𝐪|−ϵv𝐤)​|Δ​uv𝐤+𝐪⟩=\hfil\displaystyle\quad\left(H_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}^{{\bf k}+{\bf q}}+\alpha\sum_{v^{\prime}}|u_{v^{\prime}}^{{\bf k}+{\bf q}}\rangle\langle u_{v^{\prime}}^{{\bf k}+{\bf q}}|-\epsilon_{v}^{\bf k}\right)|\Delta u_{v}^{{\bf k}+{\bf q}}\rangle=\hfill
−[1−∑v′|uv′𝐤+𝐪⟩​⟨uv′𝐤+𝐪|]​Δ​vS​C​F𝐪​|uv𝐤⟩,(33)\hfil\displaystyle\hfill-\left[1-\sum_{v^{\prime}}|u_{v^{\prime}}^{{\bf k}+{\bf q}}\rangle\langle u_{v^{\prime}}^{{\bf k}+{\bf q}}|\right]\;\Delta v_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}^{\bf q}|u_{v}^{\bf k}\rangle,\quad(33)

where v′v^{\prime} runs over the occupied states at 𝐤+𝐪{\bf k}+{\bf q}, uv𝐤u_{v}^{\bf k} and Δ​uv𝐤+𝐪\Delta u_{v}^{{\bf k}+{\bf q}} are the periodic parts of the unperturbed wave-function and of the 𝐤+𝐪{\bf k}+{\bf q} Fourier component of its first-order correction, respectively, and the coordinate-representation kernel of the operator HS​C​F𝐤+𝐪H_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}^{{\bf k}+{\bf q}}, hS​C​F𝐤+𝐪​(𝐫,𝐫′)=⟨𝐫|HS​C​F𝐤+𝐪|𝐫′⟩h_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}^{{\bf k}+{\bf q}}({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime})=\langle{\bf r}|H_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}^{{\bf k}+{\bf q}}|{\bf r}^{\prime}\rangle, is defined in terms of the kernel of the SCF hamiltonian, hS​C​F(0)​(𝐫,𝐫′)=⟨𝐫|HS​C​F|𝐫′⟩h_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}^{(0)}({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime})=\langle{\bf r}|H_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}|{\bf r}^{\prime}\rangle, by the relation:

hS​C​F𝐤+𝐪(𝐫,𝐫′)=e−i(𝐤+𝐪)⋅𝐫hS​C​F0(𝐫,𝐫′)ei⁡(𝐤+𝐪)⋅𝐫′.h_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}^{{\bf k}+{\bf q}}({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime})={\rm e}^{-i({\bf k}+{\bf q})\cdot{\bf r}}h_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}^{0}({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime}){\rm e}^{i({\bf k}+{\bf q})\cdot{\bf r}^{\prime}}. (34)

Eq. (II.3.1) shows that the time-consuming step of the self-consistent process, Eq. (30), can be carried on working on lattice-periodic functions only, and the corresponding numerical workload is therefore independent of the wave-length of the perturbation.

Let us now see how the other two steps of the self-consistent process, Eqs. (23) and (II.3), can be carried on in a similar way by treating each Fourier component of the perturbing potential and of the charge-density response independently. The Fourier components of any real function (such as Δ​n\Delta n and Δ​v\Delta v) with wave-vectors 𝐪{\bf q} and −𝐪-{\bf q} are complex conjugate of each other: Δ​n−𝐪​(𝐫)=(Δ​n𝐪​(𝐫))∗\Delta n^{-{\bf q}}({\bf r})=(\Delta n^{\bf q}({\bf r}))^{*}, and similarly for the potential. Because of time-reversal symmetry, a similar results applies to wave-functions: Δ​uv𝐤+𝐪​(𝐫)=(Δ​uv−𝐤−𝐪​(𝐫))∗\Delta u^{{\bf k}+{\bf q}}_{v}({\bf r})=(\Delta u^{-{\bf k}-{\bf q}}_{v}({\bf r}))^{*}. Taking into account these relations, the Fourier component of the charge-density response at wave-vector 𝐪{\bf q} are obtained from Eq. (23):

Δnv𝐪(𝐫)=4∑𝐤​vuv𝐤∗(𝐫)Δuv𝐤+𝐪(𝐫).\Delta n^{\bf q}_{v}({\bf r})=4\sum_{{\bf k}v}u^{{\bf k}*}_{v}({\bf r})\Delta u^{{\bf k}+{\bf q}}_{v}({\bf r}). (35)

Eq. (II.3) is a linear relation between the self-consistent variation of the potential and the variation of the electron charge-density distribution. The Fourier component of the self-consistent potential response reads:

Δ​vS​C​F𝐪​(𝐫)=Δ​v𝐪​(𝐫)\displaystyle\Delta v_{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}^{\bf q}({\bf r})=\Delta v^{\bf q}({\bf r}) +\displaystyle+ e2∫Δ​n𝐪​(𝐫′)|𝐫−𝐫′|e−i𝐪⋅(𝐫−𝐫′)d𝐫′\displaystyle e^{2}\int{\Delta n^{\bf q}({\bf r}^{\prime})\over|{\bf r}-{\bf r}^{\prime}|}{\rm e}^{-i{\bf q}\cdot({\bf r}-{\bf r}^{\prime})}d{\bf r}^{\prime} (36)
+d​vx​c​(n)d​n|n=n⁡(𝐫)​Δ​n𝐪​(𝐫).\displaystyle+\left.{dv_{xc}(n)\over dn}\right|_{n=n({\bf r})}\Delta n^{\bf q}({\bf r}).

The sampling of the BZ needed for the evaluation of (35) is analogous to that needed for the calculation of the unperturbed electron charge density, (16), and it requires in most cases an equal number of discrete 𝐤{\bf k} points. An exception to this rule occurs when calculating the response of insulators to macroscopic electric fields—as discussed in Sec. II.3.2—and for the calculation of phonons in metals in the presence of Kohn anomalies—as discussed in Sec. II.3.4.

In conclusion, Eqs. (II.3.1), (35), and (36) form a set of self-consistent relations for the charge-density and wave-function linear response to a perturbation of a wave-vector, 𝐪{\bf q}, which can be solved in terms of lattice-periodic functions only, and which is decoupled from all the other sets of similar equations holding for other Fourier components of a same perturbation. Thus, perturbations of different periodicity can be treated independently of each other with a numerical workload which is, for each perturbation, of the same order as that needed for the unperturbed system.

II.3.2 Homogeneous electric fields

The electron density response to a homogeneous (macroscopic) electric field requires a special treatment. In fact, several electrostatic properties of an infinite solid are strictly speaking ill-defined in the long wave-length limit because the electrostatic potential describing a homogeneous electric field E, (VE(𝐫)=eE⋅𝐫V_{{}_{\textbf{{E}}}}({\bf r})=e\textbf{{E}}\cdot{\bf r}), is both unbound from below and incompatible with Born-von-Kármán periodic boundary conditions. In the linear regime, however, these pathologies can be efficiently treated in an elementary way. As in the harmonic approximation the lattice-dynamical properties of polar insulators depend for long wave-lengths on the linear response to a homogeneous electric field (see Sec.II.4.2), we will limit here our analysis to the linear regime only and postpone the discussion of non-linear electrostatic effects to Sec. II.6.

From a mathematical point of view, the main difficulty in treating macroscopic electric fields stems from the fact that the position operator, 𝐫{\bf r}, is ill-defined in a periodic system and so are its matrix elements between wave-functions satisfying Born-von-Kármán boundary conditions. The wave-function response to a given perturbation, Eq. (28), however, only depends on the off-diagonal matrix elements of the perturbing potential between eigen-functions of the unperturbed Hamiltonian. Such matrix elements are indeed well defined even for a macroscopic electric field, as it can be seen by re-writing them in terms of the commutator between 𝐫{\bf r} and the unperturbed Hamiltonian, which is a lattice-periodic operator:

⟨ψm|𝐫|ψn⟩=⟨ψm|[HS​C​F,𝐫]|ψn⟩ϵm−ϵn,∀m≠n.\langle\psi_{m}|{\bf r}|\psi_{n}\rangle={\langle\psi_{m}|[H_{\scriptscriptstyle SCF},{\bf r}]|\psi_{n}\rangle\over\epsilon_{m}-\epsilon_{n}},\quad\forall\ m\neq n. (37)

If the self-consistent potential acting on the electrons is local, the above commutator is simply proportional to the momentum operator:

[HS​C​F,𝐫]=−ℏ2m​∂∂𝐫.\left[H_{\scriptscriptstyle SCF},{\bf r}\right]=-{\hbar^{2}\over m}{\partial\over\partial{\bf r}}. (38)

Otherwise, the commutator will contain an explicit contribution from the non-local part of the potential [Hx1, BGT, Hx2].

When calculating the response of a crystal to an applied electric field, E0\textbf{{E}}_{0}, one must consider that the screened field acting on the electrons is:

E=E0−4​π​P,\textbf{{E}}=\textbf{{E}}_{0}-4\pi\textbf{{P}}, (39)

where P is the electronic polarization linearly induced by the screened (i.e. self-consistent) field, E:

P=−eV∫V𝐫ΔEn(𝐫)d𝐫.{\textbf{{P}}}=-{e\over V}\int_{V}{\bf r}\Delta^{\textbf{{E}}}n({\bf r})d{\bf r}. (40)

In addition to the macroscopic screening, expressed by Eq. (39), the density response to an external macroscopic electric field, E0\textbf{{E}}_{0}, also involves microscopic Fourier components,

ΔE​n​(𝐫)=4​∑n=1N/2ψn∗​(𝐫)​ΔE​ψn​(𝐫),\Delta^{\textbf{{E}}}n({\bf r})=4\sum_{n=1}^{N/2}\psi_{n}^{*}({\bf r})\Delta^{\textbf{{E}}}\psi_{n}({\bf r}), (41)

responsible for the so called local fields, that must be taken into account in the self-consistent procedure.

Eq. (40) is of course well defined for any finite system. The electric polarization of a macroscopic piece of matter, however, is ill defined in that it depends on the details of the charge distribution at the surface of the sample. Nevertheless, the polarization linearly induced by a given perturbation is well defined, and Eq. (40) can in fact be recast into a boundary-insensitive form [Littlewood]. To see this, we use Eq. (23) and we obtain from Eq. (40):

Pα\displaystyle\textsf{P}_{\alpha} =\displaystyle= −4​eV∑n=1N/2⟨ψn|rα|ΔEψn⟩\displaystyle-{4e\over V}\sum_{n=1}^{N/2}\langle\psi_{n}|r_{\alpha}|\Delta^{\textbf{{E}}}\psi_{n}\rangle
=\displaystyle= −4​eV∑n=1N/2∑m=N/2+1∞⟨ψn​|[HS​C​F,rα]||ψm⟩(ϵn−ϵm)⟨ψm|ΔEψn⟩,\displaystyle-{4e\over V}\sum_{n=1}^{N/2}\sum_{m=N/2+1}^{\infty}{\langle\psi_{n}|[H_{\scriptscriptstyle SCF},r_{\alpha}]||\psi_{m}\rangle\over(\epsilon_{n}-\epsilon_{m})}\langle\psi_{m}|\Delta^{\textbf{{E}}}\psi_{n}\rangle,

where the subscript α\alpha indicates Cartesian components. Let us introduce the wave-function ψ¯nα​(𝐫)\bar{\psi}_{n}^{\alpha}({\bf r}) defined as:

ψ¯nα​(𝐫)=∑m≠nψm​(𝐫)​⟨ψm|[HS​C​F,rα]|ψn⟩(ϵm−ϵn).\bar{\psi}_{n}^{\alpha}({\bf r})=\sum_{m\neq n}\psi_{m}({\bf r}){\langle\psi_{m}|[H_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}},r_{\alpha}]|\psi_{n}\rangle\over(\epsilon_{m}-\epsilon_{n})}. (43)

ψ¯\bar{\psi} satisfies an equation of the same kind as Eq. (30) with the perturbing potential on its right-hand side replaced by [HS​C​F,rα][H_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}},r_{\alpha}]:

(HS​C​F−ϵn)​|ψ¯nα⟩=Pc​[HS​C​F,rα]​|ψn⟩.(H_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}-\epsilon_{n})|\bar{\psi}_{n}^{\alpha}\rangle=P_{c}[H_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}},r_{\alpha}]|\psi_{n}\rangle. (44)

The induced polarization, Eq. (), can be recast into the form:

Pα=−4​eV∑n=1N/2⟨ψ¯nα|ΔEψn⟩,\textsf{P}_{\alpha}=-{4e\over V}\sum_{n=1}^{N/2}\langle\bar{\psi}_{n}^{\alpha}|\Delta^{\textbf{{E}}}\psi_{n}\rangle, (45)

where the anti-hermitian character of the commutator has been used.

The first-order correction to a crystal wave-function due to a perturbing homogeneous electric field, E, is given by the response to the full, macroscopic and microscopic, perturbation:

(HS​C​F−ϵn)|ΔEψn⟩=−e∑αEα|ψ¯nα⟩\hfil\displaystyle\quad(H_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}-\epsilon_{n})|\Delta^{\textbf{{E}}}\psi_{n}\rangle=-e\sum_{\alpha}\textsf{E}_{\alpha}|\bar{\psi}_{n}^{\alpha}\rangle\hfill
−Pc​Δ​Vl​f​|ψn⟩,(46)\hfil\displaystyle\hfill-P_{c}\Delta V^{lf}|\psi_{n}\rangle,\quad(46)

where:

Δ​Vl​f​(𝐫)=e2​∫ΔE​n​(𝐫′)|𝐫−𝐫′|​d​𝐫′\hfil\displaystyle\quad\Delta V^{lf}({\bf r})=e^{2}\int{\Delta^{\textbf{{E}}}n({\bf r}^{\prime})\over|{\bf r}-{\bf r}^{\prime}|}d{\bf r}^{\prime}\hfill
+d​vx​c​(n)d​n|n=n⁡(𝐫)​ΔE​n​(𝐫).(47)\hfil\displaystyle\hfill+\left.{dv_{xc}(n)\over dn}\right|_{n=n({\bf r})}\Delta^{\textbf{{E}}}n({\bf r}).\quad(47)

The terms of the sum appearing in (45) implicitly behave as the inverse of the difference between a conduction and a valence energy eigenvalue to the third power, ∼(ϵc−ϵv)−3\sim(\epsilon_{c}-\epsilon_{v})^{-3}. One of the energy denominators results from the standard first-order perturbation calculation of the perturbed wave function, ΔE​ψn\Delta^{\textbf{{E}}}\psi_{n}, Eq. (28). A second energy denominator comes from the term ψ¯\bar{\psi} in the right-hand side of Eq. (II.3.2), which requires by itself the solution of a linear equation analogous to that of first-order perturbation theory, Eq. (44). The third energy denominator comes from the ψ¯\bar{\psi}, which appears explicitly in the bracket of Eq. (45). This dependence of the terms of the sum upon the direct gaps at different 𝐤{\bf k} points of the BZ may require a rather fine sampling of the BZ when the fundamental gap is small. In these cases, the number of 𝐤{\bf k} points needed to compute the dielectric constant is substantially larger than that needed by a standard unperturbed calculation [raman, Hx1, piezoSdG].

The self-consistent cycle defined by Eqs. (39-II.3.2) can be performed starting from a given external macroscopic electric field, E0\textbf{{E}}_{0}, and updating at each iteration the macroscopic and microscopic part of electronic density response and the perturbing potential, via Eqs. (45), (39), (41), and (II.3.2); then solve Eq. (II.3.2) for ΔE​ψ\Delta^{\textbf{{E}}}\psi and repeat. However, for computational purposes, it is more convenient and simple to keep the value of the screened electric field, E, fixed and let only the microscopic components of the potential vary during the the iterative procedure, that is reached simply iterating Eq. (II.3.2), (41) and (II.3.2). The macroscopic polarization is then calculated only at the end when self-consistency is achieved using Eq. (45). Physically, this is equivalent to calculating the polarization response to a given screened electric field, E, instead of the response to the bare electric field E0\textbf{{E}}_{0}.

The electronic contribution to the dielectric tensor, ϵ∞α​β\epsilon^{\alpha\beta}_{\infty}, for the general (low-symmetry) case, can be derived from simple electrostatics. Using Eq. (39) and the definition of ϵ∞α​β\epsilon^{\alpha\beta}_{\infty}, one has:

E0​α=(Eα+4​π​Pα)=∑βϵ∞α​β​Eβ.\textsf{E}_{0\alpha}=(\textsf{E}_{\alpha}+4\pi\textsf{P}_{\alpha})=\sum_{\beta}\epsilon^{\alpha\beta}_{\infty}\textsf{E}_{\beta}. (48)

Using Eq. (45) to calculate the polarization induced in the α\alpha direction when a field is applied in the β\beta direction, one finally obtains:

ϵ∞α​β=δα​β−16​π​eV​Eβ​∑n=1N/2⟨ψ¯nα|ΔEβ​ψn⟩.\epsilon^{\alpha\beta}_{\infty}=\delta_{\alpha\beta}-{16\pi e\over V\textsf{E}_{\beta}}\sum_{n=1}^{N/2}\langle\bar{\psi}_{n}^{\alpha}|\Delta^{\textsf{E}_{\beta}}\psi_{n}\rangle. (49)

II.3.3 Relation to the variational principle

The KS equations are the Euler equations which solve the Hohenberg-Kohn variational principle. The equations of DFPT introduced in Sec. II.3 can be seen as a set of equations which solve approximately the variational principle when the external potential is perturbed. Alternatively, these equations can be considered as those which minimize exactly an approximate energy functional [GonzeCG, Gonze1, Gonze3]. To see this point in some detail, let us consider the energy functional as depending explicitly on the set of KS orbitals, ψ≡{ψn}\psi\equiv\{\psi_{n}\} (assumed to be real) and parametrically on the external potential, V⁡(𝐫)V({\bf r}):

E[ψ;V]=−2ℏ22​m∑n=1N/2∫ψn(𝐫)∂2ψn​(𝐫)∂𝐫2d𝐫\hfil\displaystyle\quad E[\psi;V]=-2{\hbar^{2}\over 2m}\sum_{n=1}^{N/2}\int\psi_{n}({\bf r}){\partial^{2}\psi_{n}({\bf r})\over\partial{\bf r}^{2}}d{\bf r}\hfill
+∫V(𝐫)n(𝐫)d𝐫+e22∫n⁡(𝐫)​n​(𝐫′)|𝐫−𝐫′|d𝐫d𝐫′\hfil\displaystyle+\int V({\bf r})n({\bf r})d{\bf r}+{e^{2}\over 2}\int{n({\bf r})n({\bf r}^{\prime})\over|{\bf r}-{\bf r}^{\prime}|}d{\bf r}d{\bf r}^{\prime}
+Ex​c​[n⁡(𝐫)].(50)\hfil\displaystyle\hfill+E_{xc}[n({\bf r})].\quad(50)

The functional derivative of the above functional with respect to ψn\psi_{n} is:

δ​Eδ​ψn​(𝐫)=2​HS​C​F​ψn​(𝐫).{\delta E\over\delta\psi_{n}({\bf r})}=2H_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}\psi_{n}({\bf r}). (51)

The Euler equations thus read:

HS​C​F​|ψn⟩=∑m=1N/2Λn​m​|ψm⟩,H_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}|\psi_{n}\rangle=\sum_{m=1}^{N/2}\Lambda_{nm}|\psi_{m}\rangle, (52)

where the Λ\Lambda’s are a set of Lagrange multipliers introduced so as to enforce the ortho-normality of the ψ\psi’s. Eqs. (52) are invariant with respect to a unitary transformation within the manifold of the ψ\psi’s, so that the usual KS equation, Eq. (15), is recovered in the representation which diagonalizes the Λ\Lambda matrix.

Let us now indicate by ψ(0)\psi^{(0)} the solutions of the KS equations corresponding to a particular choice of the external potential, V(0)​(𝐫)V^{(0)}({\bf r}) (the unperturbed potential), and let us indicate by Δ​V\Delta V and Δ​ψ\Delta\psi the differences between the actual potential and orbitals and their unperturbed values. The energy functional, Eq. (II.3.3), can be equally seen as depending on Δ​ψ\Delta\psi and Δ​V\Delta V: E≡E⁡[{ψ(0)+Δ​ψ};V(0)+Δ​V].E\equiv E[\{\psi^{(0)}+\Delta\psi\};V^{(0)}+\Delta V]. We now consider the approximate functional, E(2)E^{(2)}, which is obtained from EE by truncating its Taylor expansion in terms of Δ​ψ\Delta\psi and Δ​V\Delta V to second order:

E(2)​[{Δ​ψ};Δ​V]=E⁡[{ψ(0)};V(0)]+∫δ​Eδ​V​(𝐫)​Δ​V​(𝐫)​𝑑𝐫\hfil\displaystyle\quad E^{(2)}[\{\Delta\psi\};\Delta V]=E[\{\psi^{(0)}\};V^{(0)}]+\int{\delta E\over\delta V({\bf r})}\Delta V({\bf r})d{\bf r}\hfill
+∑n=1N/2∫δ​Eδ​ψn​(𝐫)Δψn(𝐫)d𝐫\hfil\displaystyle+\sum_{n=1}^{N/2}\int{\delta E\over\delta\psi_{n}({\bf r})}\Delta\psi_{n}({\bf r})d{\bf r}
+12∑n=1N/2∫δ2​Eδ​ψn​(𝐫)​δ​V​(𝐫′)Δψn(𝐫)ΔV(𝐫′)d𝐫d𝐫′\hfil\displaystyle+{1\over 2}\sum_{n=1}^{N/2}\int{\delta^{2}E\over\delta\psi_{n}({\bf r})\delta V({\bf r}^{\prime})}\Delta\psi_{n}({\bf r})\Delta V({\bf r}^{\prime})d{\bf r}d{\bf r}^{\prime}
+12∑n,m=1N/2∫δ2​Eδ​ψn​(𝐫)​δ​ψm​(𝐫′)Δψn(𝐫)Δψm(𝐫′)d𝐫d𝐫′,(53)\hfil\displaystyle\hfill+{1\over 2}\sum_{n,m=1}^{N/2}\int{\delta^{2}E\over\delta\psi_{n}({\bf r})\delta\psi_{m}({\bf r}^{\prime})}\Delta\psi_{n}({\bf r})\Delta\psi_{m}({\bf r}^{\prime})d{\bf r}d{\bf r}^{\prime},\hfill\hbox to0.0pt{\hss(53)}

where we have omitted the second derivative with respect to VV because EE is linear in VV. Besides Eq. (51), the required functional derivatives are:

δ​Eδ​V​(𝐫)|ψ=ψ(0)\displaystyle{\delta E\over\delta V({\bf r})}\biggr|_{\psi=\psi^{(0)}} =\displaystyle= n(0)​(𝐫)\displaystyle n^{(0)}({\bf r}) (54)
δ2​Eδ​ψn​(𝐫)​δ​V​(𝐫′)|ψ=ψ(0)\displaystyle{\delta^{2}E\over\delta\psi_{n}({\bf r})\delta V({\bf r}^{\prime})}\biggr|_{\psi=\psi^{(0)}} =\displaystyle= 2​ψn(0)​(𝐫)​δ​(𝐫−𝐫′)\displaystyle 2\psi^{(0)}_{n}({\bf r})\delta({\bf r}-{\bf r}^{\prime}) (55)
δ2​Eδ​ψn​(𝐫)​δ​ψm​(𝐫′)|ψ=ψ(0)\displaystyle{\delta^{2}E\over\delta\psi_{n}({\bf r})\delta\psi_{m}({\bf r}^{\prime})}\biggr|_{\psi=\psi^{(0)}} =\displaystyle= 2​hS​C​F(0)​(𝐫,𝐫′)\displaystyle 2h^{(0)}_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime}) (56)
+4​K​(𝐫,𝐫′)​ψn(0)​(𝐫)​ψm(0)​(𝐫′),\displaystyle+4K({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime})\psi^{(0)}_{n}({\bf r})\psi^{(0)}_{m}({\bf r}^{\prime}),

where:

K⁡(𝐫,𝐫′)=e2|𝐫−𝐫′|+δ2​Ex​cδ​n​(𝐫)​δ​n​(𝐫′),K({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime})={e^{2}\over|{\bf r}-{\bf r}^{\prime}|}+{\delta^{2}E_{xc}\over\delta n({\bf r})\delta n({\bf r}^{\prime})}, (57)

and hS​C​F(0)​(𝐫,𝐫′)h^{(0)}_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime}) is the kernel of the unperturbed KS Hamiltonian. The energy functional, Eq. (II.3.3), must be minimized under the constraints that the resulting solutions lead to an orthonormal set of occupied states:

⟨ψn(0)+Δ​ψn|ψm(0)+Δ​ψm⟩=δn​m.\langle\psi^{(0)}_{n}+\Delta\psi_{n}|\psi^{(0)}_{m}+\Delta\psi_{m}\rangle=\delta_{nm}. (58)

This leads to the Euler equations:

HS​C​F(0)​|Δ​ψn⟩−∑m=1N/2Λn​m​|Δ​ψm⟩=\hfil\displaystyle\quad H^{(0)}_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}|\Delta\psi_{n}\rangle-\sum_{m=1}^{N/2}\Lambda_{nm}|\Delta\psi_{m}\rangle=\hfill
−Δ​VS​C​F​|ψn(0)⟩+∑m=1N/2(Λn​m−ϵn​δn​m)​|ψm(0)⟩,(59)\hfil\displaystyle\hfill-\Delta V_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}|\psi^{(0)}_{n}\rangle+\sum_{m=1}^{N/2}(\Lambda_{nm}-\epsilon_{n}\delta_{nm})|\psi^{(0)}_{m}\rangle,\quad(59)

where the Λ\Lambda’s are a set of Lagrange multipliers introduced so as to enforce the constraints, Eq. (58), and

Δ​VS​C​F​(𝐫)=Δ​V​(𝐫)\hfil\displaystyle\quad\Delta V_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}({\bf r})=\Delta V({\bf r})\hfill
+2∑n=1N/2∫d𝐫′K(𝐫,𝐫′)ψn(0)(𝐫′)Δψn(𝐫′)(60)\hfil\displaystyle\hfill+2\sum_{n=1}^{N/2}\int d{\bf r}^{\prime}K({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime})\psi^{(0)}_{n}({\bf r}^{\prime})\Delta\psi_{n}({\bf r}^{\prime})\quad(60)

is the first-order variation of the self-consistent potential. We now project both sides of Eq. (II.3.3) onto ψk(0)\psi^{(0)}_{k}. Taking into account that by Eq. (58) ⟨Δ​ψn|ψk(0)⟩=𝒪⁡(Δ2)\langle\Delta\psi_{n}|\psi^{(0)}_{k}\rangle={\cal O}(\Delta^{2}), to linear order in Δ\Delta one obtains:

Λm​n−ϵn​δn​m=⟨ψm(0)|Δ​VS​C​F|ψn(0)⟩.\Lambda_{mn}-\epsilon_{n}\delta_{nm}=\langle\psi^{(0)}_{m}|\Delta V_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}|\psi^{(0)}_{n}\rangle. (61)

To linear order in Δ\Delta, Eq. (II.3.3) can thus be cast into the form:

(HS​C​F(0)−ϵn)​|Δ​ψn⟩\displaystyle(H^{(0)}_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}-\epsilon_{n})|\Delta\psi_{n}\rangle =\displaystyle= −Δ​VS​C​F​|ψn(0)⟩\displaystyle-\Delta V_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}|\psi^{(0)}_{n}\rangle (62)
+∑m=1N/2|ψm(0)⟩​⟨ψm(0)|Δ​VS​C​F|ψn(0)⟩\displaystyle\mbox{}+\sum_{m=1}^{N/2}|\psi^{(0)}_{m}\rangle\langle\psi^{(0)}_{m}|\Delta V_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}|\psi^{(0)}_{n}\rangle
=\displaystyle= −Pc​Δ​VS​C​F​|ψn(0)⟩,\displaystyle-P_{c}\Delta V_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}|\psi^{(0)}_{n}\rangle,

which is essentially the same as Eq. (30). The set of perturbed orbitals, {Δ​ψ}\{\Delta\psi\}, is the solution of NN coupled linear systems whose dimension is the size of the basis set, MM (Eq. (62) or Eq. (30), where the coupling comes from the dependence of the self-consistent potential on all the orbitals). Alternatively, it can be seen as a huge linear system of dimension M×N/2M\times N/2, which is obtained by inserting the expression for Δ​VS​C​F\Delta V_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}, Eq. (II.3.3), into Eqs. (62) or (30). The latter is naturally derived from the minimization of the functional E(2)E^{(2)}, Eq. (II.3.3), which is quadratic.

This variational approach shows that the error on the functional to be minimized, Eq. (II.3.3), is proportional to the square of the error on the minimization variables, Δ​ψ\Delta\psi. This fact can be exploited in the calculation of the second-order mixed derivatives, Eq. (22). It can be shown that a variational expression can be constructed for mixed derivatives as well [GonzeCG, Gonze3].

II.3.4 Metals

Density-functional perturbation theory, as presented above, is directly applicable to metals, provided the (electronic) temperature vanishes, so that a clear cut separation between occupied and empty states is possible. In this case, however, the number of kk points needed to correctly represent the effect of the Fermi surface would be very large. Practical implementations of DFPT to metallic systems have been discussed by ? and by ?, in the pseudo-potential formalism, and by ?, in the Linearized Muffin-Tin Orbital framework. In the following, we will closely follow the formulation of ? which is based on the smearing technique for dealing with Fermi-surface effects.

In the smearing approach each KS energy level is broadened by a smearing function:

δσ​(ϵ)=1σ​δ~​(ϵ/σ),\delta_{\sigma}(\epsilon)={1\over\sigma}\tilde{\delta}(\epsilon/\sigma), (63)

where δ~​(x)\tilde{\delta}(x) is any function that integrates to 1—so that δσ​(ϵ)\delta_{\sigma}(\epsilon) tends to the Dirac δ\delta function in the limit of vanishing smearing width, σ\sigma. Many kinds of smearing functions, δ~​(x)\tilde{\delta}(x), can be used: Fermi-Dirac broadening,33 3 In this case the broadening function is the derivative of the Fermi-Dirac distribution function: δ~​(x)=12​(1+cosh⁡(x))−1\tilde{\delta}(x)={1\over 2}\left(1+\cosh(x)\right)^{-1}. Lorentzian, Gaussian [smearing], Gaussian combined with polynomials [MP], or cold smearing [Nicola-coldsmearing] functions, to recall just a few of those used in the literature. While the choice of a given smearing function is to some extent a matter of personal taste and computational convenience, the specific choice of the Fermi-Dirac broadening allows one to explicitly account for the effects of a finite temperature (T=σ/kBT=\sigma/k_{B}), when needed. The (local) density of states resulting from the broadened energy levels will be the original density of states, convoluted with the smearing function:

n⁡(𝐫,ϵ)=∑n1σ​δ~​(ϵ−ϵnσ)​|ψn​(𝐫)|2,n({\bf r},\epsilon)=\sum_{n}{1\over\sigma}\tilde{\delta}\left(\frac{\epsilon-\epsilon_{n}}{\sigma}\right)|\psi_{n}({\bf r})|^{2}, (64)

where the sum refers both to the discrete 𝐤{\bf k}-vector index and to band and spin indices, for all bands. From this basic quantity the electron density follows:

n⁡(𝐫)=∫−∞ϵFn⁡(𝐫,ϵ)​𝑑ϵ=∑nθ~​(ϵF−ϵnσ)​|ψn​(𝐫)|2,n({\bf r})=\int_{-\infty}^{\epsilon_{F}}n({\bf r},\epsilon)d\epsilon=\sum_{n}\tilde{\theta}\left({\epsilon_{F}-\epsilon_{n}\over\sigma}\right)|\psi_{n}({\bf r})|^{2}, (65)

where θ~​(x)=∫−∞xδ~​(y)​𝑑y\tilde{\theta}(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x}\tilde{\delta}(y)dy is a smooth approximation to the step function, and the Fermi energy is determined by the normalization to the total number of electrons,

N=∫−∞ϵFn⁡(ϵ)​𝑑ϵ=∑nθ~​(ϵF−ϵnσ).N=\int_{-\infty}^{\epsilon_{F}}n(\epsilon)d\epsilon=\sum_{n}\tilde{\theta}\left({\epsilon_{F}-\epsilon_{n}\over\sigma}\right). (66)

The advantage of this procedure is that after convolution the (modified) local density of states can be computed accurately on a discrete grid of points in the BZ, provided that the average separation between neighboring eigenvalues is small with respect to the broadening width, σ\sigma.

Given the definition of the local density of states, Eq. (64), the consistent way to define the auxiliary KS kinetic-energy functional—or its analogue in the finite temperature theory [mermin]—is through the Legendre transform of the single-particle energy integral:

Ts​[n]\displaystyle T_{s}[n] =\displaystyle= ∫−∞ϵFϵ​n​(ϵ)​𝑑ϵ−∫VS​C​F​(𝐫)​n​(𝐫)​𝑑𝐫\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\epsilon_{F}}\epsilon n(\epsilon)d\epsilon-\int V_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}({\bf r})n({\bf r})d{\bf r} (67)
=\displaystyle= ∑n[−ℏ22​mθ~(ϵF−ϵnσ)∫ψn∗(𝐫)∂2ψn​(𝐫)∂𝐫2d𝐫\displaystyle\sum_{n}\left[-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\tilde{\theta}\left(\frac{\epsilon_{F}-\epsilon_{n}}{\sigma}\right)\int\psi^{*}_{n}({\bf r}){\partial^{2}\psi_{n}({\bf r})\over\partial{\bf r}^{2}}d{\bf r}\right.
+σθ~1(ϵF−ϵnσ)],\displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\left.+\sigma\tilde{\theta}_{1}\left(\frac{\epsilon_{F}-\epsilon_{n}}{\sigma}\right)\right],

where θ~1​(x)=∫−∞xy​δ~​(y)​𝑑y\tilde{\theta}_{1}(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x}y\tilde{\delta}(y)dy. Note that when a finite electronic temperature is considered the KS auxiliary functional, Ts​[n]T_{s}[n], contains both the kinetic energy and the entropy contribution to the electronic free energy of the independent particle system. These two contributions appear separately in the last expression for Ts​[n]T_{s}[n] in Eq. (67) where it can be verified that for Fermi-Dirac broadening θ~1​(x)=f​log⁡(f)+(1−f)​log⁡(1−f)\tilde{\theta}_{1}(x)=f{\log}(f)+(1-f){\log}(1-f), with f=θ~​(x)f=\tilde{\theta}(x) as required. With the definitions above, for any kind of smearing function, the usual KS equations follow from the minimization of the total energy. The price to be paid for the computational simplicity of the smearing approach is that the computed total energy depends on the chosen broadening width and results for finite broadening widths must be corrected for, unless the shape of the smearing function is such as to reduce this dependence within acceptable values. Various discussions of this issue can be found in the literature [MP, Nicola-coldsmearing, SdGmetalli, DeVita].

Forces and other first-order energy derivatives can be computed in the usual way from Eqs. (8) and (21) which only require the knowledge of the unperturbed electronic density. Similarly second-order derivatives are computed from Eq. (22) where also the first order variation of the density is needed. Direct variation of Eq. (65) provides the required expression for Δ​n​(𝐫)\Delta n({\bf r}):

Δn(𝐫)=∑nθ~F,n[ψn∗(𝐫)Δψn(𝐫)+c.c.]\hfil\displaystyle\quad\Delta n({\bf r})=\sum_{n}\tilde{\theta}_{F,n}\left[\psi^{*}_{n}({\bf r})\Delta\psi_{n}({\bf r})+c.c.\right]\hfill
+∑n|ψn(𝐫)|2δ~F,n(ΔϵF−Δϵn),(68)\hfil\displaystyle\hfill+\sum_{n}|\psi_{n}({\bf r})|^{2}\tilde{\delta}_{F,n}(\Delta\epsilon_{F}-\Delta\epsilon_{n}),\quad(68)

where we have defined θ~n,m=θ~​((ϵn−ϵm)/σ)\tilde{\theta}_{n,m}=\tilde{\theta}((\epsilon_{n}-\epsilon_{m})/\sigma) and δ~n,m=(1/σ)​δ~​((ϵn−ϵm)/σ)\tilde{\delta}_{n,m}=(1/\sigma)\tilde{\delta}((\epsilon_{n}-\epsilon_{m})/\sigma). The last term in Eq. (II.3.4) accounts for possible changes in occupation numbers induced by shifts in the single particle energies (Δ​ϵn=⟨ψn|Δ​VS​C​F|ψn⟩\Delta\epsilon_{n}=\langle\psi_{n}|\Delta V_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}|\psi_{n}\rangle), as well as in the Fermi energy of the system. Whether this term is present or not depends on the thermodynamic ensemble used: it is absent if the chemical potential is kept fixed, whereas it might be present if it is the number of electrons which is fixed. Even in this last case the Fermi energy is unaffected by the perturbation to linear order, unless the perturbation is lattice-periodic (monochromatic with 𝐪=0{\bf q}=0). Let us neglect this term for the time being and come back to it at the end of the section.

Substituting in Eq. (II.3.4) the definition for Δ​ψn​(𝐫)\Delta\psi_{n}({\bf r}) from standard perturbation theory, Eq. (28), and exploiting the symmetry between the two contributions in square brackets, one obtains the following well known expression for the first-order variation of the electronic density in a metal:

Δ​n​(𝐫)=∑n,mθ~F,n−θ~F,mϵn−ϵm\hfil\displaystyle\quad\Delta n({\bf r})=\sum_{n,m}\frac{\tilde{\theta}_{F,n}-\tilde{\theta}_{F,m}}{\epsilon_{n}-\epsilon_{m}}\hfill
×ψn∗​(𝐫)​ψm​(𝐫)​⟨ψm|Δ​VS​C​F|ψn⟩,(69)\hfil\displaystyle\hfill\times~\psi^{*}_{n}({\bf r})\psi_{m}({\bf r})\langle\psi_{m}|\Delta V_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}|\psi_{n}\rangle,\quad(69)

where the term in Δ​ϵn\Delta\epsilon_{n} in Eq. (II.3.4) has become the n=mn=m term in the above sum and the incremental ratio (θ~F,n−θ~F,m)/(ϵn−ϵm)(\tilde{\theta}_{F,n}-\tilde{\theta}_{F,m})/(\epsilon_{n}-\epsilon_{m}) must be substituted with its limit, −δ~F,n-\tilde{\delta}_{F,n}, whenever ϵm→ϵn\epsilon_{m}\rightarrow\epsilon_{n}. This limit is always finite for any finite broadening line-width, or temperature, and this expression is therefore numerically stable even in the presence of vanishingly small virtual excitation energies.

In order to avoid the double sum over occupied and unoccupied states we use the relation θ~​(x)+θ~​(−x)=1\tilde{\theta}(x)+\tilde{\theta}(-x)=1 and the symmetry between ii and jj to get

Δ​n​(𝐫)=2​∑n,mθ~F,n−θ~F,mϵn−ϵm​θ~m,n\hfil\displaystyle\quad\Delta n({\bf r})=2\sum_{n,m}\frac{\tilde{\theta}_{F,n}-\tilde{\theta}_{F,m}}{\epsilon_{n}-\epsilon_{m}}\tilde{\theta}_{m,n}\hfill
×ψn∗​(𝐫)​ψm​(𝐫)​⟨ψm|Δ​VS​C​F|ψn⟩,(70)\hfil\displaystyle\hfill\times~\psi^{*}_{n}({\bf r})\psi_{m}({\bf r})\langle\psi_{m}|\Delta V_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}|\psi_{n}\rangle,\quad(70)

where the sum over the first index can be limited to the states that have non negligible occupation. This expression can be further simplified, avoiding the explicit sum over the second index, by re-writing it as:

Δ​n​(𝐫)=2​∑nψn∗​(𝐫)​Δ​ψn​(𝐫),\Delta n({\bf r})=2\sum_{n}\psi_{n}^{*}({\bf r})\Delta\psi_{n}({\bf r}), (71)

where the Δ​ψn\Delta\psi_{n}’s satisfy the equation

[HS​C​F+Q−ϵn]​Δ​ψn=−[θ~F,n−Pn]​Δ​VS​C​F​|ψn⟩,\left[H_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}+Q-\epsilon_{n}\right]\Delta\psi_{n}=-\left[\tilde{\theta}_{F,n}-P_{n}\right]\Delta V_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}|\psi_{n}\rangle, (72)

with

Q=∑kαk​|ψk⟩​⟨ψk|,Pn=∑mβn,m​|ψm⟩​⟨ψm|,Q=\sum_{k}\alpha_{k}|\psi_{k}\rangle\langle\psi_{k}|,\quad\quad P_{n}=\sum_{m}\beta_{n,m}|\psi_{m}\rangle\langle\psi_{m}|,
βn,m=θ~F,n​θ~n,m+θ~F,m​θ~m,n+αm​θ~F,n−θ~F,mϵn−ϵm​θ~m,n.\beta_{n,m}=\tilde{\theta}_{F,n}\tilde{\theta}_{n,m}+\tilde{\theta}_{F,m}\tilde{\theta}_{m,n}+\alpha_{m}\frac{\tilde{\theta}_{F,n}-\tilde{\theta}_{F,m}}{\epsilon_{n}-\epsilon_{m}}\tilde{\theta}_{m,n}. (73)

In the above equations the αk\alpha_{k}’s are chosen in such a way that the QQ operator makes the linear system, Eq. (72), nonsingular for all non vanishing Δ​ψn\Delta\psi_{n}. A possible simple choice is

αk=max⁡(ϵF+Δ−ϵk,0),\alpha_{k}={\max}(\epsilon_{F}+\Delta-\epsilon_{k},0), (74)

with Δ≈3÷4​σ\Delta\approx 3\div 4\sigma. Another, even simpler, choice is to set αk\alpha_{k} equal to the occupied bandwidth plus, say, 3​σ3\sigma for all partially occupied states and zero when the state is totally unoccupied. It can be easily verified that since αk\alpha_{k} vanishes when ψk\psi_{k} is unoccupied then also βn,m\beta_{n,m} vanishes when any of its indices refers to an unoccupied state. Therefore the QQ and PP operators involve only the small number of partially filled bands and the first-order variation of the wave functions and of the charge density can be computed avoiding any explicit reference to the unoccupied states, much in the same way as for insulating materials. In fact, if the above scheme is applied to an insulator using a smearing width much smaller than its fundamental band gap, all the metallic equations, Eqs. (71-73), reduce numerically to their insulating analogues, Eqs. (23) and (30).

The expression for the charge density linearly induced by a given perturbation, Eqs. (II.3.4) and (II.3.4), involves an energy denominator which vanishes for metals. In one dimension, this vanishing denominator gives rise to a divergence in the screening of perturbations whose wave-vector is twice the Fermi momentum, 2​kF2k_{F}. This divergence is smeared in two dimensions and suppressed in three dimensions by volume effects. However, if the topology of the Fermi surface is such that two finite portions of it are parallel and connected by a wave-vector which for convenience we will name 2​kF2k_{F} (nesting), the screening to perturbations of wave-vector 2​kF2k_{F} will diverge even in three dimension. This is the physical mechanism giving rise to Kohn anomalies in the vibrational spectra of certain metals. The sampling of the BZ necessary to evaluate the sum over (partially) occupied states in Eqs. (II.3.4) and (II.3.4) is in ordinary cases similar to that needed to calculate the unperturbed charge-density distribution. Near a Kohn anomaly, however, a fine sampling of the Fermi surface is necessary and the number of needed points in the BZ is correspondingly larger.

Periodic (𝐪=0{\bf q}=0) perturbations may induce a shift of the Fermi energy. In this case Eq. (71) must be modified as:

Δ​n​(𝐫)=2​∑nψn∗​(𝐫)​Δ​ψn​(𝐫)+n⁡(𝐫,ϵF)​Δ​ϵF,\Delta n({\bf r})=2\sum_{n}\psi_{n}^{*}({\bf r})\Delta\psi_{n}({\bf r})+n({\bf r},\epsilon_{F})\Delta\epsilon_{F}, (75)

all other technical details remaining unchanged. In order to find out the appropriate value of the Fermi energy shift let us examine the perturbation in the 𝐪→0{\bf q}\rightarrow 0 limit. Let us consider the Fourier transform of the self-consistent perturbing potential ΔVS​C​F(𝐪)=1/V∫ΔVS​C​F(𝐫)e−i𝐪⋅𝐫d𝐫\Delta V_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}({\bf q})=1/V\int\Delta V_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}({\bf r})e^{-i{\bf q}\cdot{\bf r}}d{\bf r}. Its macroscopic (𝐪≈0{\bf q}\approx 0) component reads:

Δ​VS​C​F​(𝐪)=Δ​V​(𝐪)+4​π​e2q2​Δ​n​(𝐪)+d​vx​cd​n​Δ​n​(𝐪),\Delta V_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}({\bf q})=\Delta V({\bf q})+\frac{4\pi e^{2}}{q^{2}}\Delta n({\bf q})+{dv_{xc}\over dn}\Delta n({\bf q}), (76)

where the last term is the exchange-correlation contribution, Δ​V​(𝐪)=−4​π​e2q2​Δ​ne​x​t​(𝐪)\Delta V({\bf q})=-\frac{4\pi e^{2}}{q^{2}}\Delta n_{ext}({\bf q}) is the macroscopic electrostatic component of the external perturbing potential, and Δ​ne​x​t​(𝐪)\Delta n_{ext}({\bf q}) is finite in the 𝐪→0{\bf q}\rightarrow 0 limit. On the other hand the macroscopic component of the density response is

Δ​n​(𝐪)=−n⁡(ϵF)​Δ​VS​C​F​(𝐪)+Δ​nl​f​(𝐪),\Delta n({\bf q})=-n(\epsilon_{F})\Delta V_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}({\bf q})+\Delta n^{lf}({\bf q}), (77)

where Δ​nl​f\Delta n^{lf} is the density response to the non-macroscopic (local fields) components of the self-consistent potential. As Δ​nl​f\Delta n^{lf} and the DOS at the Fermi energy, n⁡(ϵF)n(\epsilon_{F}), are both finite, Δ​VS​C​F\Delta V_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}} and Δ​n\Delta n must not diverge when 𝐪→0{\bf q}\rightarrow 0 otherwise Eqs. (76) and (77) could not be satisfied at the same time. This implies, from Eq. (76), macroscopic charge neutrality for the perturbed system, that is Δ​ne​x​t​(𝐪)=Δ​n​(𝐪)+𝒪⁡(q2)\Delta n_{ext}({\bf q})=\Delta n({\bf q})+{\cal O}(q^{2}) for 𝐪≈0{\bf q}\approx 0; a condition that in turn implies in Eq. (77)

Δ​VS​C​F​(𝐪)=−Δ​ne​x​t​(𝐪)−Δ​nl​f​(𝐪)n⁡(ϵF)+𝒪⁡(q2).\Delta V_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}({\bf q})=-\frac{\Delta n_{ext}({\bf q})-\Delta n^{lf}({\bf q})}{n(\epsilon_{F})}+{\cal O}(q^{2}). (78)

The lattice periodic (𝐪=0{\bf q}=0) result can be obtained by taking the 𝐪→0{\bf q}\rightarrow 0 limit of the above equations. In this case however, it is costumary to set arbitrarily to zero the macroscopic electrostatic component of the self-consistent potential and the charge neutrality condition is thus enforced by a compensating shift in the Fermi energy, equal and opposite to the above result:

Δ​ϵF=Δ​ne​x​t​(𝐪=0)+∫n⁡(𝐫,ϵF)​Δ​VS​C​F​(𝐫)​𝑑𝐫n⁡(ϵF).\Delta\epsilon_{F}=\frac{\Delta n_{ext}({\bf q}=0)+\int n({\bf r},\epsilon_{F})\Delta V_{{\scriptscriptstyle SCF}}({\bf r})d{\bf r}}{n(\epsilon_{F})}. (79)

II.4 Phonons

II.4.1 Vibrational states in crystalline solids

In crystalline solids, the nuclear positions appearing in the definition of the IFC’s, Eq. (5), are labelled by an index, II, which indicates the unit cell to which a given atom belongs, ll, and the position of the atom within that unit cell, ss: I≡{l,s}I\equiv\{l,s\}. The position of the II-th atom is thus:

𝐑I≡𝐑l+τττs+𝐮s​(l),{\bf R}_{I}\equiv{\bf R}_{l}+\hbox{\kern-0.24994pt\hbox{$\tau$}\kern-4.37154pt\kern 0.50003pt\hbox{$\tau$}\kern-4.37154pt\kern-0.24994pt\raise 0.43304pt\hbox{$\tau$}}_{s}+{\bf u}_{s}(l), (80)

where 𝐑l{\bf R}_{l} is the position of the ll-th unit cell in the Bravais lattice, τττs\hbox{\kern-0.24994pt\hbox{$\tau$}\kern-4.37154pt\kern 0.50003pt\hbox{$\tau$}\kern-4.37154pt\kern-0.24994pt\raise 0.43304pt\hbox{$\tau$}}_{s} is the equilibrium position of the ss-th atom in the unit cell, and 𝐮s​(l){\bf u}_{s}(l) indicates the deviation from equilibrium of the nuclear position. Because of translational invariance, the matrix of the IFC’s, Eq. (II.1), depends on ll and mm only through the difference 𝐑≡𝐑l−𝐑m{\bf R}\equiv{\bf R}_{l}-{\bf R}_{m}:

Cs​tα​β​(l,m)≡∂2E∂usα​(l)​∂utβ​(m)=Cs​tα​β​(𝐑l−𝐑m),C^{\alpha\beta}_{st}(l,m)\equiv{\partial^{2}E\over\partial u^{\alpha}_{s}(l)\partial u^{\beta}_{t}(m)}=C^{\alpha\beta}_{st}({\bf R}_{l}-{\bf R}_{m}), (81)

where the greek super-scripts indicate Cartesian components. The Fourier transform of Cs​tα​β​(𝐑)C^{\alpha\beta}_{st}({\bf R}) with respect to 𝐑{\bf R}, C~s​tα​β​(𝐪)\widetilde{C}^{\alpha\beta}_{st}({\bf q}), can be seen as the second derivative of the BO energy surface with respect to the amplitude of a lattice distortion of definite wave-vector:

C~s​tα​β(𝐪)≡∑𝐑e−i𝐪⋅𝐑Cs​tα​β(𝐑)\hfil\displaystyle\quad\widetilde{C}^{\alpha\beta}_{st}({\bf q})\equiv\sum_{\bf R}{\rm e}^{-i{\bf q}\cdot{\bf R}}C^{\alpha\beta}_{st}({\bf R})\hfill

where NcN_{c} is the number of unit cells in the crystal, and the vector 𝐮s​(𝐪){\bf u}_{s}({\bf q}) is defined by the distortion pattern:

𝐑I​[𝐮s​(𝐪)]=𝐑l+τττs+𝐮s​(𝐪)​ei​𝐪⋅𝐑l.{\bf R}_{I}[{\bf u}_{s}({\bf q})]={\bf R}_{l}+\hbox{\kern-0.24994pt\hbox{$\tau$}\kern-4.37154pt\kern 0.50003pt\hbox{$\tau$}\kern-4.37154pt\kern-0.24994pt\raise 0.43304pt\hbox{$\tau$}}_{s}+{\bf u}_{s}({\bf q}){\rm e}^{i{\bf q}\cdot{\bf R}_{l}}. (83)

det|1Ms​Mt​C~s​tα​β​(𝐪)−ω2​(𝐪)|=0.\det\left|{1\over\sqrt{M_{s}M_{t}}}\widetilde{C}^{\alpha\beta}_{st}({\bf q})-\omega^{2}({\bf q})\right|=0. (84)

Translational invariance can be alternatively stated in this context by saying that a lattice distortion of wave-vector 𝐪{\bf q} does not induce a force response in the crystal at wave-vector 𝐪′≠𝐪{\bf q}^{\prime}\neq{\bf q}, in agreement with the analysis carried out in Sec. II.3.1. Because of this property, IFC’s are most easily calculated in reciprocal space and, when they are needed in direct space, they can be readily obtained by Fourier transform (see Sec. II.4.3).

The reciprocal-space expression for the matrix of IFC’s, Eq. (II.1), is the sum of an electronic and of an ionic contribution:
